clue.text: Drink and drug producer takes a bit of opium

indicators.note: one word taking another holds it inside, so the plant's name swallows the letter

parts.note: the coca plant is the source of cocaine

indicators.note: a small bit of the word opium is just its opening letter

explanation.surface: A grower of drug crops also dabbles in a little opium.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot chocolate drink made from powdered cacao beans is the everyday sense.

clue.text: Dance crazes going to extremes over virtuoso passage

indicators.note: read as a verb, crazes means drives mad, so the letters of dance are thrown into disorder
in a down clue over means turned upside down, so the pair reads from bottom to top

parts.note: A to Z are the two extremes of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Fashionable dances go wild before a showy musical solo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going to' is just a link; 'extremes' are the two ends of the alphabet, and 'over' flips them in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadenza is the elaborate solo section where a soloist shows off technique, usually near the end of a concerto movement.

clue.text: Dogs inside — sticks outside

indicators.note: the sticks go round the outside of the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: walking sticks are canes
inside can mean in, as in at home

explanation.surface: Keep the dogs indoors and their sticks out in the garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Canine is the scientific word for a dog, so the plural names dogs generally.

clue.text: Arsenal gutted — Everton's midfield is on the ball

indicators.note: a gutted word has lost all its insides, so only its first and last letters stay
the midfield of a word is its central letters, here the middle three of the club name

explanation.surface: A football report: Arsenal devastated while Everton's midfielders are sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal and Everton are English football clubs. The central three letters of EVERTON give ERT.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the ball is an idiom for being quick, attentive and wide awake.

clue.text: The setter, two zulus (adult) and a cardinal — it might be between the first and second

definitions.text: it might be between the first and second

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as me
Zulu is the radio code word for Z, so two of them are ZZ
A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult
a cardinal number such as nine

explanation.surface: A cast list: the setter, two Zulus, an adult and a cardinal.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is about floors of a building: between the first and second floor.
explanation.definitionFit: A mezzanine is an intermediate storey placed between two main floors of a building.

clue.text: Blokes crowd round to help girl

indicators.note: the men gather on both sides of the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: blokes is British slang for men
help means aid

explanation.surface: A group of men gather to assist a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Maiden is an old-fashioned word for a young unmarried woman.

clue.text: Unstable Nazi stands on head — this is crazy stuff

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece stands on top of the second
unstable letters are not fixed in place, so they are rearranged

parts.note: a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: A deranged fascist does a headstand, which is certainly madness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this is' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Zaniness is comic craziness, the quality of being wildly silly.

clue.text: To become thin you had a latish breakfast according to text?

parts.note: a breakfast taken rather late might be at ten
you had, written in text-message shorthand, is u ate

explanation.surface: A dieter asks whether a late breakfast helps them slim, in text-speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'according to text' says the pieces are spelt as in text messages: AT TEN plus U ATE, the sentence 'u ate at ten' with its halves swapped into answer order.
explanation.definitionFit: To attenuate is to make or become thinner or weaker, from the Latin for thin.

clue.text: One new sample of tea perhaps needs identification — flavourless

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
a sip is a small taste of a drink such as tea

explanation.surface: A tea taster's single new sample needs labelling because it tastes of nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needs' just links the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Insipid means lacking taste or interest; bland and watery.

clue.text: English bank as an alternative for Roosevelt say?

parts.note: an aircraft banks when it tilts, so bank means lean
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: An English bank offers an alternative for President Roosevelt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say?' flags an example: the Roosevelt meant is the First Lady, not Franklin or Theodore.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleanor Roosevelt, wife of Franklin, is a famous bearer of the first name, so she is one example.

clue.text: Daniel Defoe wastes the enemy — 'Fierce beast' is a weed

parts.note: Dan is the standard abbreviation for the biblical book of Daniel

indicators.note: to waste something is to get rid of it, so these letters are thrown away

parts.note: a foe is an enemy
the lion is the classic fierce beast

explanation.surface: The author of Robinson Crusoe kills an enemy and a wild animal turns out to be a weed.
explanation.walkthrough: Daniel Defoe was the author of Robinson Crusoe. 'wastes' removes FOE from DEFOE, leaving DE.
explanation.definitionFit: The yellow-flowered plant that lawn owners dig out is the classic example of a garden weed.

clue.text: To give a shock takes time? — Smack!

indicators.note: one word taking another holds it inside

parts.note: to tase someone is to hit them with an electric stun gun

explanation.surface: Is a stun gun shock time-consuming, compared with a slap?
explanation.definitionFit: A smack of something is a slight flavour of it, so the noun means a trace or flavour.

clue.text: E.g. de Valois shows us one, the opposite of gross, with ten dancing around

indicators.note: the jumbled ten goes round the outside of the other pieces
letters that are dancing are moving about, so they are rearranged

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
a net amount is the opposite of a gross one, after deductions

explanation.surface: A ballerina demonstrates how to take one, deduct from gross, and twirl ten.
explanation.walkthrough: Dame Ninette de Valois founded Britain's Royal Ballet; the shuffled letters split to wrap around the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Ninette is the first name of de Valois, the Irish-born dancer who founded the Royal Ballet.

clue.text: I get knocked down by one in news deal when cycling

definitions.text: I get knocked down by one

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new, read here as the start of news
taken as written

indicators.note: cycling a word moves letters from one end round to the other

parts.note: deal is a softwood, especially pine

explanation.surface: Someone reads a news story about a deal that was knocked on the head.
explanation.walkthrough: Cycling PINE moves its last letter to the front, giving EPIN.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the skittles in a bowling game is knocked over by a single ball, as the clue's speaker describes.

clue.text: When groups come together in capital

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
sets are groups

explanation.surface: Groups combine in a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come together in' just links the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm's capital is its money and property, its holdings of value.

clue.text: Con man rooks with tickets for wrestling

indicators.note: wrestlers twist and grapple, so these letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: R is the chess abbreviation for rook, so two rooks are RR

explanation.surface: A swindler cheats people out of tickets for a wrestling match.
explanation.definitionFit: A con man is a swindler, someone who deceives people for gain.

clue.text: False witness statement: "Man restricted my movements"?

definitions.meaning: a witness who says they defame someone is saying '...'
the Isle of Man is an island, so a resident there finds travel limited by the sea

explanation.surface: A witness claims a man restrained them, but the statement is false.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone living on the Isle of Man is an island dweller; split after the first letter it is 'I slander'.

clue.text: Open pie cooked with last of ginger and spicy sausage

indicators.note: cooked suggests the letters are worked over and rearranged
the last of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A recipe: an open pie cooked with a little ginger and spiced sausage.
explanation.definitionFit: Peperoni is a spicy Italian dried sausage, often sliced onto pizza; this is a variant spelling.

clue.text: Coppers surround northern mountain range

indicators.note: the coins go round the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: British copper coins are pennies

explanation.surface: Police officers close in on a mountain range in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' looks like police but means copper coins.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pennines are the chain of hills running down northern England, called its backbone.

clue.text: Have sons got into groups of friends?

indicators.note: the sons got into the other piece, so that letter goes inside it

parts.note: a posse is informal for a group of friends
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A parent asks whether their sons have joined gangs of mates.
explanation.definitionFit: To possess something is to own or hold it.

clue.text: Serious knight getting promoted to head is most miserly

indicators.note: the letter is promoted, moving up to the head of the word

parts.note: earnest means serious
N is the chess abbreviation for knight

explanation.surface: A solemn knight is made head of the order and turns out to be a terrible miser.
explanation.definitionFit: Near is an old British sense of stingy, so the superlative means most tight-fisted.

clue.text: I like to pick a rabbit say and put in for boiling

indicators.note: the jumbled word is put inside the other piece

parts.note: a rabbit is an example of a pet

indicators.note: boiling stirs things up, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A cook chooses a rabbit and throws it in the pot.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is nit-picking, not choosing: the speaker likes to pick holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A fussy stickler for detail likes to pick holes and nits, as the speaker says.

clue.text: Idiotic lapse by current head of nursing in A&E

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the letters for the hospital department

parts.note: A and E, accident and emergency, is the British hospital casualty department
a moral lapse is a sin
I is the physics symbol for electric current

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A foolish mistake by the senior nurse in the emergency department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is a link. A&E is the British name for the emergency room.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine means as stupid as an ass, from the Latin for donkey.

clue.text: Corrupt senator's crime?

indicators.note: corrupt suggests the letters are spoiled and rearranged

parts.note: the possessive ending is dropped, leaving the word senator

explanation.surface: The crime of a crooked politician.
explanation.walkthrough: '?' signals the definition is an example: betraying one's country is one crime a corrupt senator might commit.
explanation.definitionFit: Betraying one's country or ruler is a serious offence, so it is one example of a crime.

clue.text: Maybe 9 section acting as flipping emergency room

parts.note: qua is Latin for in the capacity of, acting as

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the letters read backwards

explanation.surface: A doctor complains that a hospital unit has become a blasted casualty ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' is both a mild British curse and the reversal signal. '9' is the number, not clue 9.
explanation.definitionFit: Nine is three times three, so it is an example of a perfect square number.

clue.text: Say 'Boom'! — a setback for moose in animation

parts.note: a boom on a sailing ship is a spar

indicators.note: a setback sets the word back, reading it in reverse

parts.note: the elk is the European name for the moose

explanation.surface: An explosion sound in a cartoon, as an animated moose suffers a reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks Boom as an example of a spar.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparkle means liveliness and vivacity, so it can stand for animation.

clue.text: Ingredient of tonic wine, one of five used in place of whiskey

indicators.note: one piece is used instead of a letter, replacing it

parts.note: Whiskey is the radio code word for W
a quin is one of quintuplets, five babies born together

explanation.surface: A recipe for a drink in which one of five spirits replaces whiskey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tonic wine' looks like one phrase; the definition is just the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Quinine gives tonic water its bitter taste, so it is one of the drink's ingredients.

clue.text: One scam succeeded showing pictures linked to apps

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
a con is a scam
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, used in family trees

explanation.surface: A single fraud worked, judging by the pictures linked to some apps.
explanation.definitionFit: On a phone or computer screen, the small images you tap to launch programs are called this.

clue.text: Specialist after releasing pressure put in effort

indicators.note: once the letter for pressure is released, it is let go from the word

parts.note: a specialist is an expert
P is the physics symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: A specialist made an effort after letting off pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: To exert oneself is to strive or apply force.

clue.text: Musically presented stories or airs too ornate

indicators.note: something ornate is elaborately reworked, so the letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: Tales set to music, or tunes that are too elaborate.
explanation.definitionFit: Oratorios are large-scale musical works for voices and orchestra telling a story, often a biblical one.

clue.text: Chiefly sad or solemn in nature perhaps?

indicators.note: chiefly picks the chief or first letter of the next word
perhaps suggests the letters may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Is someone chiefly sad, or simply grave by nature?
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' is a link here, though it looks like part of 'sad or solemn'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturnine describes a gloomy, grave temperament, once attributed to the planet Saturn's influence.

clue.text: Birds in flight seen from base in hide

indicators.note: the base letter is put in the middle of the other piece

parts.note: an animal's hide is its skin
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: Birdwatchers in a hide spot a flock flying overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hide' suggests a birdwatcher's shelter, but it means animal skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A skein is the collective noun for wild geese flying in formation.
